explanation:
## Solving $\pi P = \pi$

Column by column:

$$\begin{aligned}
j = 1:&\quad \tfrac12\pi_1 + \tfrac13\pi_2 + 0 = \pi_1 &&\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_2 = \tfrac32\pi_1\\
j = 3:&\quad 0 + \tfrac13\pi_2 + \tfrac34\pi_3 = \pi_3 &&\Longrightarrow\quad \tfrac14\pi_3 = \tfrac13\pi_2 = \tfrac12\pi_1 \;\Longrightarrow\; \pi_3 = 2\pi_1
\end{aligned}$$

The equation for $j=2$ is then automatically satisfied — it always is, because the columns of $\pi(P - I)$ sum to zero.

Normalising, $\pi_1\bigl(1 + \tfrac32 + 2\bigr) = 1$, so $\pi_1 = \tfrac29$ and

$$\pi = \Bigl(\tfrac29,\ \tfrac13,\ \tfrac49\Bigr), \qquad \pi_3 = \frac49 .$$

A check: $\tfrac29 + \tfrac39 + \tfrac49 = 1$, and $\pi_2 = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac29 + \tfrac13\cdot\tfrac13 + \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac49 = \tfrac19+\tfrac19+\tfrac19 = \tfrac13$.

## What the numbers mean

Three readings of the same vector, and all three are theorems:

- **Equilibrium.** Start the chain with distribution $\pi$ and it has distribution $\pi$ at every later time.
- **The limit.** The chain is irreducible, aperiodic and (being finite and irreducible) positive recurrent, so $\P(X_n = j) \to \pi_j$ from **any** starting distribution.
- **Occupation time and return time.** The long-run fraction of time spent at $j$ is $\pi_j$, and $\pi_j = 1/\mu_j$ where $\mu_j$ is the mean return time. Here $\mu_3 = \tfrac94 = 2.25$ steps and $\mu_1 = \tfrac92 = 4.5$.

State 3 has the largest share because it is the stickiest: once there, the chain stays with probability $\tfrac34$ each step, so visits to it last a geometric number of steps with mean 4.

## Rows and columns, once more

The three equations sum down **columns**, which is the opposite of the hitting-probability equations $h_i = \sum_j p_{i,j} h_j$ in §3.3. The reason is worth saying: $\pi_j$ is the equilibrium chance of being at $j$, so it is assembled from every way of **arriving** at $j$ — the arrows pointing in. A hitting probability is assembled from every way of **leaving** $i$ — the arrows pointing out.

## Why one equation is always redundant

If $\pi$ solves $\pi P = \pi$ then so does $c\pi$ for every constant $c$, so the solution space of the linear system is at least one-dimensional and the system cannot have full rank. That is why the normalisation $\sum_j \pi_j = 1$ is not an extra constraint being imposed on a determined system — it is what picks one point out of a line of solutions.

Three states, three equations, one redundant, one normalisation: two independent conditions for two free ratios.
